Peripheral enhancement can improve neuromuscular transmission, increase gastrointestinal or bladder activity, reverse nondepolarising neuromuscular blockade, or increase parasympathetic tone. Centrally penetrant inhibitors can modestly support cholinergic signalling in selected neurodegenerative syndromes but do not restore lost neurons. Increased transmitter also produces muscarinic and nicotinic toxicity, so therapeutic context and dose determine whether enhancement is useful.

Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase and can produce prolonged inhibition. With time, the enzyme-organophosphate complex may age and become resistant to reactivation. Excess acetylcholine causes secretions, sweating, vomiting, diarrhoea, miosis, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia or variable cardiovascular effects, muscle fasciculation followed by weakness, and central agitation, seizures, or coma. Respiratory failure can combine airway secretions, bronchospasm, central depression, and neuromuscular paralysis. Contaminated clothing and skin may continue exposure.

Management of severe cholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning begins with protection from contamination and support of airway, oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation. Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors and is titrated to reversal of dangerous muscarinic features, especially bronchial secretion and bronchospasm, rather than to pupil size alone. An oxime can reactivate some phosphorylated enzyme before ageing and is particularly relevant to nicotinic weakness, although effectiveness depends on compound and timing. Benzodiazepines treat seizures. None of these measures replaces decontamination and supportive care.

Muscarinic antagonists prevent parasympathetic acetylcholine from activating effector receptors. Atropine is a prototypical competitive antagonist. Effects include reduced secretion and sweating, mydriasis with cycloplegia, tachycardia, bronchodilation, reduced gastrointestinal motility, and urinary retention. The response depends on baseline tone: blocking vagal input markedly accelerates a resting heart with strong vagal influence but may have less effect during maximal sympathetic activation. At low doses, complex presynaptic and central actions can occasionally produce responses that do not fit a simple monotonic model.

Different antagonists are selected by route, kinetics, and tissue access. Inhaled quaternary agents concentrate effect in airways with limited systemic absorption. Eye preparations create local mydriasis or cycloplegia. Bladder-selective strategies aim to reduce detrusor overactivity while limiting dry mouth, constipation, cognitive effects, and impaired sweating. Centrally active agents may reduce motion-related vestibular signalling or selected movement symptoms. Selectivity is always relative; increasing exposure erodes the advantage.

Antimuscarinic toxicity often presents with dry mucosae, hot skin from impaired sweating, mydriasis, blurred near vision, tachycardia, reduced bowel sounds, urinary retention, agitation, delirium, hallucinations, and hyperthermia. Young children and older adults are particularly vulnerable to temperature and cognitive effects. Many antihistamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, bladder drugs, and over-the-counter products contribute to cumulative anticholinergic burden. Toxicity may therefore arise without a prescription labelled as an autonomic drug.

Ganglionic drugs influence both sympathetic and parasympathetic transmission, so organ effects reflect whichever division supplies dominant resting tone. Blocking ganglia can produce vasodilation and postural hypotension because vascular tone is predominantly sympathetic, while causing tachycardia because the resting heart often has parasympathetic dominance. It can also produce dry mouth, cycloplegia, constipation, urinary retention, and impaired sexual function. This lack of organ selectivity largely limits therapeutic use but illustrates why autonomic pharmacology must be interpreted through prevailing tone.

Presynaptic receptors and cotransmitters further complicate cholinergic signalling. Autoreceptors can restrain additional transmitter release. Adenosine triphosphate, peptides, nitric oxide, and other mediators may be released with classical transmitters. High-frequency stimulation can recruit a different mixture than low-frequency activity. Drugs acting on synthesis, storage, release, degradation, or feedback therefore change the temporal pattern of transmission, not merely the amount of acetylcholine at one receptor.

Cholinergic effects in the eye illustrate linked anatomy. Iris sphincter contraction causes miosis, while ciliary-muscle contraction releases zonular tension so the lens rounds for near vision. This also opens trabecular outflow pathways and can lower intraocular pressure. Muscarinic blockade causes mydriasis and cycloplegia and may impair drainage in an anatomically narrow angle. A useful local ocular effect can therefore provoke systemic absorption or a dangerous pressure response unless anatomy, dose, and administration technique are considered.

Clinical reasoning is clearest when it follows the synapse. Identify whether the relevant site is central, ganglionic, postganglionic muscarinic, or skeletal neuromuscular. Determine whether treatment should increase or reduce acetylcholine, whether the anatomical pathway is intact, and which other organs express the affected receptors. Then consider duration, reversibility, route, reflex compensation, and cumulative burden. The same cholinergic mechanism can relieve urinary retention, worsen obstruction, improve muscle strength, cause respiratory secretions, or produce delirium according to where and how strongly it acts.

## TTS module 2: Adrenergic transmission and pharmacology

Sympathetic signalling prepares organs for changing demand rather than producing one universal fight-or-flight state. Preganglionic cholinergic fibres activate ganglia and adrenal medulla. Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline from varicosities distributed along target tissue, while adrenal chromaffin cells release adrenaline and some noradrenaline into blood. The resulting response depends on receptor subtype, transmitter concentration, basal tone, circulating hormones, and reflex compensation. The same sympathomimetic can therefore raise pressure, slow the pulse reflexly, dilate bronchi, alter metabolism, and reduce gastrointestinal activity at once.

Catecholamine synthesis begins when tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to dihydroxyphenylalanine, the rate-limiting regulated step. Aromatic amino-acid decarboxylase forms dopamine. Vesicular transport moves dopamine into storage vesicles, where dopamine beta-hydroxylase forms noradrenaline. In adrenal medulla, cytosolic phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase uses a methyl donor to form adrenaline and is promoted by high local glucocorticoid exposure from adrenal cortex. Transmitters are then stored with adenosine triphosphate, peptides, and proteins until calcium-triggered exocytosis.

Termination differs from cholinergic transmission. Reuptake into the presynaptic neuron through the noradrenaline transporter is the major immediate mechanism at many sympathetic synapses. Recycled transmitter returns to vesicles or is metabolised by monoamine oxidase. Catechol-O-methyltransferase acts in extraneuronal tissues, and metabolites are further processed and excreted. Because transmitter can diffuse and re-enter terminals, blockade of uptake prolongs and spatially broadens signalling. Metabolic enzyme inhibition may have larger effects when transmitter synthesis, dietary amines, or other monoamines increase.

Alpha one receptors mainly couple through phospholipase C and intracellular calcium. They contract vascular smooth muscle, radial iris muscle, bladder outlet, and selected sphincters, and can promote glandular and metabolic responses. Vascular alpha one activation raises peripheral resistance and venous tone. Increased arterial pressure activates baroreceptors and can produce reflex bradycardia, so the observed heart rate is not a pure receptor readout. Local nasal or ocular vasoconstriction reduces congestion or redness but repeated exposure can cause ischaemia or rebound congestion.

Alpha two receptors commonly inhibit adenylyl cyclase and reduce transmitter release from presynaptic terminals. They also occur postsynaptically in brainstem, platelets, pancreas, vessels, and other tissues. Central alpha two agonism reduces sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate and pressure while producing sedation and dry mouth. Peripheral vascular activation can initially raise pressure, especially after rapid systemic exposure, before central effects dominate. Abrupt withdrawal after adaptation can release sympathetic activity and cause rebound hypertension.

Beta one receptors increase cyclic AMP and calcium handling in the heart, raising rate, conduction, contractility, and relaxation. They also promote renin release from juxtaglomerular cells. Greater contractility and rate increase oxygen demand, which can be harmful when coronary supply is limited. Beta one selectivity is relative and decreases as concentration rises. Endogenous catecholamine effects also depend on innervation: noradrenaline released at cardiac terminals efficiently activates beta one receptors, whereas circulating adrenaline can reach beta receptors throughout the body.

Beta two receptors relax many smooth muscles through cyclic AMP-dependent pathways, producing bronchodilation, vasodilation in selected vascular beds, and uterine relaxation. They also shift potassium into cells, stimulate glycogen breakdown, and can cause tremor and tachycardia. Cardiac acceleration may result from direct loss of selectivity, reflex response to vasodilation, or both. Inhalation concentrates bronchodilation in airways but does not eliminate systemic exposure. Frequent need for a short-acting bronchodilator can signal poor control of the underlying inflammatory disease rather than a need for unlimited receptor stimulation.

Beta three receptors contribute to lipolysis, thermogenic signalling, and bladder detrusor relaxation. Dopamine receptors, although not adrenergic receptors, are relevant to catecholamine pharmacology. At lower exposure, selected dopamine-receptor effects can alter vascular and endocrine functions; at higher exposure dopamine also activates beta and then alpha receptors. The historical idea of a reliably kidney-selective dopamine dose has not translated into protection from acute kidney injury. Dose labels cannot replace measured haemodynamic and organ responses.

Direct sympathomimetics bind adrenergic receptors themselves. Adrenaline activates alpha and beta receptors, with the balance changing by concentration and tissue. It supports vascular tone, cardiac output, bronchodilation, and reduced mediator release during severe systemic allergic reactions. Noradrenaline strongly increases vascular tone and supports pressure in vasodilatory shock, while reflexes may limit tachycardia. A selective beta agonist may support cardiac output, and an alpha one agonist may raise vascular resistance. Choosing among them requires identifying the haemodynamic deficit rather than treating a low pressure number in isolation.

Indirect sympathomimetics increase endogenous catecholamine in the synapse by promoting release, reversing transport, inhibiting reuptake, or inhibiting metabolism. Their effect depends on intact nerve terminals and available transmitter stores, so repeated dosing can cause tachyphylaxis. Mixed-action drugs combine receptor agonism with transmitter release. Central stimulant effects involve additional dopamine and noradrenaline pathways and can produce wakefulness, appetite suppression, euphoria, anxiety, or psychosis according to dose and susceptibility. Peripheral effects include vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and reduced gastrointestinal function.

Alpha one antagonists reduce arteriolar and venous tone and relax smooth muscle at the bladder outlet. They can improve urinary flow when dynamic smooth-muscle tone contributes to obstruction, but they do not shrink fixed tissue or correct a mechanical lesion. First-dose and postural hypotension occur because normal sympathetic compensation on standing is impaired. Reflex tachycardia varies with receptor selectivity and kinetics. Alpha antagonism in catecholamine-secreting tumours must be planned carefully; unopposed beta stimulation before adequate alpha blockade can worsen vasoconstriction.

Beta blockers differ in beta one selectivity, intrinsic partial agonism, lipid solubility, membrane effects, elimination, and additional vasodilating properties. They reduce heart rate, contractility, renin release, and selected arrhythmias, and they modify harmful chronic adrenergic signalling in certain forms of heart failure. Benefits can emerge over time even though acute negative inotropy is possible. Abrupt cessation after receptor upregulation can provoke rebound tachycardia or ischaemia. Dose and indication determine whether a pharmacological effect is therapeutic or hazardous.

Blocking beta two receptors can increase airway resistance and interfere with rescue bronchodilation, particularly in reactive airway disease. Beta blockade can also mask adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia, although sweating may persist because it is sympathetic cholinergic. Peripheral vascular symptoms, fatigue, exercise limitation, sleep disturbance, and conduction slowing vary across patients and agents. Apparent contraindications should be interpreted by receptor selectivity, disease severity, benefit, dose, and monitoring rather than by drug-class name alone.

Adrenergic neurone blockers can inhibit synthesis, vesicular storage, or release, but broad disruption of sympathetic compensation creates orthostatic and sexual adverse effects. Monoamine oxidase inhibition increases vulnerability to interacting monoamines and certain indirectly acting drugs. Excess substrate can release noradrenaline faster than it is controlled, causing severe hypertension and hyperthermia. The interaction depends on inhibitor selectivity, reversibility, dose, intestinal and hepatic metabolism, and time since discontinuation.

Sympathomimetic toxicity is a physiological syndrome rather than a single laboratory value. Agitation, mydriasis, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, tremor, chest pain, seizures, and muscle injury can occur. Severe vasoconstriction may coexist with intravascular volume depletion. Temperature elevation reflects muscular activity, central drive, and impaired heat dissipation and requires active management. Treatment emphasises supportive care, reduced stimulation, sedation when appropriate, cooling, fluids guided by physiology, and management of specific cardiovascular complications; indiscriminate isolated receptor blockade can worsen an unstable balance.

Autonomic reflexes explain many counterintuitive findings. Vasoconstriction can slow the heart through baroreflex activation despite direct cardiac stimulation. Vasodilation can cause tachycardia despite no beta agonism. Denervation, neuropathy, ageing, spinal injury, volume depletion, and concurrent drugs alter these reflexes. Measurements over time are more informative than a single reading because direct receptor effects and compensatory responses have different onset and duration.

Adrenergic pharmacology is therefore an exercise in systems control. Identify the receptor profile, but also identify the compartment reached, endogenous transmitter supply, prevailing tone, and reflex loop. Separate pressure into cardiac output and vascular resistance, and separate cardiac output into rate and stroke volume. A drug is not simply an alpha agonist or beta blocker in the patient; it is an input into an adaptive circulation, airway, metabolic system, and brain whose response changes with context and time.

## TTS module 3: Neuromuscular transmission and local mediator pharmacology

The skeletal neuromuscular junction converts a motor-nerve action potential into muscle contraction with a large normal safety margin. Acetylcholine released from one specialised terminal crosses a narrow cleft and binds muscle nicotinic receptors densely packed on junctional folds. Sodium entry produces an endplate potential that activates nearby voltage-gated sodium channels. The muscle action potential spreads along sarcolemma and transverse tubules, triggers calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum, and initiates actin-myosin cycling. Disease or drugs can interrupt any link while leaving the others intact.

Nondepolarising neuromuscular blockers competitively occupy muscle nicotinic receptors without opening them. As occupancy rises, the endplate potential fails to reach threshold and flaccid paralysis develops. Small rapidly moving muscles may weaken before the diaphragm, while recovery can occur in a different order. These drugs do not produce unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, or sedation. A paralysed person can remain fully aware, so neuromuscular blockade must never be mistaken for anaesthesia.

Block depth can be assessed by stimulating a peripheral nerve and measuring muscle response. Repeated stimuli reveal fade when transmitter mobilisation cannot overcome receptor blockade. Quantitative monitoring is more reliable than visual or tactile estimation, and adequate apparent breathing does not guarantee recovery of pharyngeal function. Residual blockade increases airway obstruction and aspiration risk. Reversal can be achieved by increasing acetylcholine with a cholinesterase inhibitor, usually while blocking unwanted muscarinic effects, or by encapsulating selected blocker molecules with a binding agent.

Depolarising blockade is produced by a nicotinic agonist that opens endplate channels but persists longer than acetylcholine. Initial depolarisation causes visible fasciculation, followed by electrical inactivation and flaccid paralysis. With prolonged exposure, membrane and receptor behaviour changes into a later phase resembling nondepolarising block. Potassium can leave repeatedly depolarised muscle, becoming dangerous in burns, denervation, major muscle injury, prolonged immobility, or neuromuscular disease where extrajunctional receptors increase. Genetic variation in plasma cholinesterase can greatly prolong metabolism and apnoea.

Botulinum toxins cleave proteins required for cholinergic vesicle fusion. At motor terminals they produce local weakness; at autonomic cholinergic terminals they reduce secretion and smooth-muscle effects. Precisely injected small doses can treat focal overactivity, but diffusion or excessive dose can cause dysphagia, generalized weakness, or respiratory impairment. Tetanus toxin also enters motor terminals but travels centrally and blocks inhibitory transmitter release, producing disinhibition and spasm rather than peripheral flaccidity. Similar molecular machinery can therefore yield opposite syndromes according to anatomical trafficking.

Local mediators are produced near their site of action, often rapidly and transiently. They coordinate vascular tone, permeability, smooth muscle, platelets, nociception, inflammation, secretion, and cell growth. Unlike a conventional endocrine hormone, their concentration can vary sharply across micrometres and seconds. Pharmacology can block synthesis, prevent release, antagonise receptors, accelerate removal, or mimic the mediator. Because several mediators act together, suppressing one pathway may reveal another rather than abolish the response.

Histamine is stored prominently in mast-cell and basophil granules and is also produced by gastric and neural cells. Immunological cross-linking, complement fragments, physical stimuli, and selected drugs can trigger release. H one receptors promote endothelial contraction and permeability, sensory-nerve itch, bronchial and intestinal smooth-muscle contraction, and wakefulness-related central signalling. Endothelial nitric oxide contributes to vasodilation. H two receptors stimulate gastric acid secretion and contribute to cardiac and vascular effects. Additional receptor subtypes regulate neural transmitter release and immune cells.

H one antihistamines are inverse agonists that stabilise inactive receptor states. Older lipophilic agents enter the brain and can cause sedation, impaired performance, antimuscarinic effects, and postural symptoms. Newer agents are generally less centrally penetrant but are not identical in kinetics or interaction risk. They reduce histamine-mediated itch, sneezing, and wheal responses but do not reliably reverse every component of severe systemic allergy. When airway, breathing, or circulation is threatened, adrenaline addresses several life-threatening mechanisms and should not be replaced by an antihistamine.

H two antagonists reduce acid secretion by blocking parietal-cell histamine signalling. Proton-pump inhibitors act farther downstream on the final acid pump and usually suppress acid more strongly, illustrating how pathway position changes effect. Histamine release in the stomach is stimulated by neural and hormonal inputs, so receptor blockade modifies an integrated network. Chronic acid suppression can alter infection risk, nutrient handling, and feedback hormones, although the size and relevance of these effects vary by patient and duration.

Serotonin is synthesised from tryptophan and functions in brain, enteric nervous system, gastrointestinal mucosa, platelets, and vessels. Most peripheral serotonin is produced by enterochromaffin cells; platelets take it up rather than synthesise it and release it during activation. Receptor families include G-protein-coupled receptors and a ligand-gated cation channel. Different subtypes influence mood, nausea, motility, vascular tone, platelet function, and nociception. A drug described simply as serotonergic is therefore mechanistically incomplete.

Serotonin-receptor antagonists can suppress nausea arising from vagal and central pathways, while selected agonists constrict cranial vessels and inhibit neuropeptide release in migraine. Excess serotonergic activity can cause agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, autonomic instability, diarrhoea, and hyperthermia. The syndrome is favoured by combining drugs that increase synthesis, release, receptor stimulation, or reduce reuptake or metabolism. Neuromuscular findings and exposure history help distinguish it from other hyperthermic toxic syndromes.

Eicosanoids are oxygenated products of membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids. Cell activation releases arachidonic acid through phospholipase enzymes. Cyclo-oxygenases generate intermediates used to form prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane; lipoxygenases generate leukotrienes and related mediators. Products are made on demand, act locally, and are rapidly metabolised. Their balance differs among endothelium, platelets, leukocytes, kidney, gastric mucosa, reproductive tissue, and other organs.

Prostaglandins regulate pain sensitisation, fever, vascular tone, renal perfusion, gastric protection, uterine activity, and ductal patency. Prostacyclin from endothelium tends to dilate vessels and restrain platelets, whereas platelet thromboxane promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction. Leukotrienes recruit inflammatory cells, increase permeability, and can constrict airways. These summaries are context-dependent; receptor subtype and tissue determine the final effect. Synthetic analogues and receptor antagonists exploit particular pathways in obstetric, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, vascular, and ophthalmic practice.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase activity, reducing prostanoid synthesis. Analgesia and fever reduction arise partly from lower prostaglandin signalling, while anti-inflammatory effects generally require sustained exposure. The same mechanism reduces gastric mucosal defence, changes renal haemodynamics, and impairs platelet function to differing degrees. Selective inhibition can reduce some gastrointestinal injury but may disturb vascular thrombotic balance. Risk depends on dose, duration, age, kidney function, volume status, cardiovascular disease, anticoagulation, and co-medication.

Glucocorticoids suppress mediator production farther upstream by changing gene transcription, leukocyte trafficking, cytokines, and enzymes including those that liberate or process arachidonic acid. Their broad efficacy comes with broad physiological costs involving infection defence, glucose, bone, muscle, skin, mood, eyes, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression. Abrupt withdrawal after sustained systemic treatment can expose adrenal insufficiency and rebound inflammation. Local delivery reduces but does not eliminate systemic effects.

Bradykinin is generated in plasma and tissues through kallikrein-kinin pathways. It promotes vasodilation, permeability, pain, and selected smooth-muscle responses, largely through endothelial nitric oxide and prostaglandins. Angiotensin-converting enzyme degrades bradykinin as well as producing angiotensin two, so enzyme inhibition both reduces vasoconstrictor formation and increases bradykinin. Cough and rare dangerous swelling reflect this second action. Drugs can also block bradykinin receptors or kallikrein in selected swelling disorders.

Nitric oxide is synthesised from arginine by nitric-oxide synthases. Endothelial calcium-dependent production activates soluble guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle, raises cyclic GMP, and causes relaxation. Neural nitric oxide acts as a transmitter, while inducible high-output production participates in host defence and inflammatory vasodilation. Organic nitrates provide nitric-oxide-related signalling, phosphodiesterase inhibitors slow cyclic-GMP breakdown, and guanylyl-cyclase stimulators enhance the pathway. Combining strong inputs can cause profound hypotension.

Tolerance to continuous nitrate exposure involves multiple vascular and systemic adaptations, so a low-exposure interval can restore responsiveness in suitable indications. Nitric oxide is rapidly inactivated by haemoglobin and oxidants, confining much of its action locally. In oxidative stress it can form reactive nitrogen species and contribute to injury. Thus the same small molecule supports physiological endothelial control, pharmacological vasodilation, antimicrobial defence, and pathological damage according to concentration and chemical environment.

Neuromuscular and mediator pharmacology converge on one lesson: anatomical location and pathway timing matter as much as target name. Receptor blockade at a motor endplate causes paralysis without unconsciousness; histamine blockade relieves itch without treating all of anaphylaxis; cyclo-oxygenase inhibition relieves pain while removing renal and gastric protection; nitric-oxide amplification dilates desired vessels while lowering systemic pressure. Safe use follows the whole physiological circuit and anticipates what else the same intervention removes or amplifies.

# Chapter 99: Learning, Development, Cognition, Stress, and Behaviour Change

## TTS module 1: Learning, memory, and their biological foundations

Learning is a relatively durable change in knowledge, behaviour, or response tendency produced by experience. Memory is the set of processes that encode, store, stabilise, and retrieve information. Neither is a single faculty. A person can acquire a motor skill while unable to recall the practice episode, recognise a face without naming it, or remember a fact without using it effectively. Clinical assessment therefore separates sensory access, attention, encoding, retention, retrieval, language, motivation, and performance rather than interpreting every failure as loss of memory.

Habituation is reduced response to a repeated inconsequential stimulus. Sensitisation is increased responsiveness after a strong or important stimulus. These non-associative forms show that nervous systems continuously estimate significance. Habituation is not sensory fatigue: response can recover after time or a novel stimulus. Sensitisation can generalise beyond the original cue and contributes to heightened pain, vigilance, or startle after threat. At synapses, altered transmitter release and excitability can support short-term changes, while gene expression and structural remodelling support longer persistence.

Classical conditioning occurs when a previously neutral cue predicts a biologically meaningful event and comes to elicit a response. Acquisition depends on contingency, not merely temporal pairing: the cue must add information about the outcome. Extinction follows repeated cue presentation without the expected outcome, but it usually creates new inhibitory learning rather than erasing the original association. Spontaneous recovery, renewal in a different context, and reinstatement after the outcome reappears reveal that the older memory remains available.

Fear conditioning links sensory cues and contexts with defensive responses through circuits including amygdala, hippocampus, and prefrontal regions. The amygdala helps assign threat value and coordinate autonomic and behavioural output. The hippocampus represents context and relationships, while prefrontal systems can regulate expression according to safety and goals. These are interacting networks, not isolated storage boxes. Exposure-based treatment uses prediction error and inhibitory learning, and its success depends on tolerable engagement, varied safe contexts, and opportunities to learn that feared outcomes do not occur or can be managed.

Operant conditioning changes behaviour through its consequences. Reinforcement increases the future probability of behaviour; punishment decreases it. Positive means that something is added, and negative means that something is removed, not good or bad. Negative reinforcement can maintain avoidance when escape removes anxiety immediately, even though avoidance prevents corrective learning and causes long-term disability. Consequences that are immediate, reliable, and valued usually shape behaviour more strongly than delayed abstract outcomes.

Reinforcement schedules alter response patterns. Continuous reinforcement supports rapid acquisition but behaviour may extinguish quickly when reward stops. Intermittent reinforcement can make behaviour persistent, especially when the number of responses or timing is unpredictable. This helps explain durable checking, gambling, and repeated use of digital rewards. Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a goal. In health care, small achievable steps can establish self-efficacy, whereas demands far beyond current capacity may repeatedly punish effort and reduce engagement.

Observational learning allows behaviour to be acquired by watching others. Attention, retention, ability to reproduce the action, and motivation influence whether modelling changes behaviour. Social consequences matter: observing another person rewarded or harmed modifies expectation. Clinicians, family, peers, and media all model health behaviour. Instruction is more effective when the demonstrated action is feasible in the learner's environment and when feedback corrects performance rather than merely restating information.

Working memory temporarily maintains and manipulates a limited amount of information. It supports reasoning, comprehension, mental calculation, and planning. Attention selects among competing inputs, while executive control protects goals, updates contents, and switches tasks. Capacity falls with distraction, sleep deprivation, pain, anxiety, intoxication, and acute illness. Chunking uses meaningful structure to reduce burden, but expertise-specific chunks do not transfer automatically to novices. Apparent nonadherence may therefore reflect cognitive overload rather than opposition.

Declarative memory includes episodic memory for events in context and semantic memory for facts and concepts. Nondeclarative memory includes skills, habits, priming, and conditioned responses. Medial temporal structures, especially hippocampal networks, are critical for forming new declarative memories but are not the permanent repository of every detail. Distributed cortical systems support long-term representations, while basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits contribute to habits, skills, timing, and error-based adaptation.

Encoding improves when attention is active and material is elaborated, organised, connected to prior knowledge, or generated by the learner. Retrieval practice strengthens later access more effectively than repeated passive reading, and spacing study over time outperforms massed repetition for durable retention. Interleaving related problem types can improve discrimination, though it feels harder. The subjective fluency of rereading is a poor measure of learning because familiarity can rise without the ability to retrieve or apply information.

Consolidation stabilises memories after encoding. Synaptic consolidation unfolds over minutes to hours through receptor trafficking, kinase signalling, gene expression, and protein synthesis. Systems consolidation reorganises dependence across neural networks over longer periods. Sleep supports memory through coordinated changes in hippocampal and cortical activity, but effects differ by memory type and sleep stage. Sleep also restores attention and emotion regulation, so better performance after sleep does not arise from storage processes alone.

Long-term potentiation is a persistent increase in synaptic effectiveness after particular activity patterns and is one model of memory-related plasticity. At many excitatory synapses, coincident depolarisation and glutamate signalling permit calcium entry through N M D A receptors, triggering kinase pathways and insertion or modification of A M P A receptors. Stronger or repeated activation can induce gene expression and structural change. Long-term depression weakens selected synapses and is equally important for refinement, flexibility, and preventing saturation.

Plasticity follows rules of timing, neuromodulation, and network state. Dopamine can mark prediction error and motivational significance; acetylcholine can alter attention and cortical learning; noradrenaline can signal arousal and uncertainty. Stress hormones may strengthen memory for central emotional features while impairing flexible contextual recall. Plasticity is not always beneficial: persistent pain, addiction, traumatic fear, and maladaptive habits also involve learned network change. The goal is appropriate learning, not maximal plasticity.

Retrieval is reconstructive. A cue reactivates parts of a distributed representation, and current context, expectations, emotion, and later information can fill gaps. Confidence and accuracy are related imperfectly. Suggestive questioning and repeated imagination can alter recollection. Reconsolidation refers to the possibility that a reactivated memory becomes temporarily modifiable before restabilising, but boundary conditions matter and laboratory findings do not justify assuming that any memory can be deliberately rewritten.

Forgetting can reflect decay, interference, retrieval failure, or adaptive updating. Proactive interference occurs when older learning disrupts new learning; retroactive interference occurs when newer material disrupts access to older information. Similar memories compete more than distinctive ones. Retrieval cues that recreate context can help, but dependence on one context reduces transfer. Teaching should therefore vary examples and require recall under conditions resembling future use.

Memory disorders reveal process boundaries. Damage to medial temporal systems can severely impair new episodic learning while sparing immediate span, remote knowledge, or skill acquisition. Frontal dysfunction can impair strategy, source monitoring, and retrieval despite retained storage. Delirium produces fluctuating attention and global cognitive disruption, making apparent memory testing unreliable. Depression, anxiety, sleep loss, hearing impairment, medication effects, and pain can reduce encoding. A complaint of memory loss therefore requires history, function, course, and examination rather than one score.

Learning transfers poorly when knowledge is tied to surface features. Expertise develops through organised conceptual structures, repeated retrieval, feedback, and varied application, not exposure alone. Feedback is most useful when timely, specific, and directed at a controllable process. Errors can promote learning when the environment is psychologically safe and correction explains the governing rule. Excessive threat narrows attention and encourages concealment, impairing both learning and patient safety.

The biological and behavioural levels are complementary. Synaptic plasticity explains how experience can alter a circuit, while conditioning and cognitive theories describe what information is learned and when it is expressed. Neither level alone predicts a person's behaviour in a social environment. Effective medical learning and behaviour change align attention, meaningful prediction error, repeated retrieval, sleep, feedback, motivation, and opportunities to practise the desired action across contexts.

## TTS module 2: Lifespan development, cognition, and social-emotional growth

Development is continuous change produced by genes, maturation, experience, relationships, culture, and historical conditions. It is neither a rigid universal timetable nor unlimited plasticity. Skills emerge within ranges, build on earlier capacities, and can follow several viable paths. Developmental assessment asks what a person can do across domains, how abilities changed over time, what opportunities were available, and whether the pattern causes functional difficulty. A single delayed milestone does not identify a cause, while loss of an established skill is usually more concerning than late acquisition alone.

Prenatal brain development includes cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, axon guidance, synapse formation, and selective cell death. After birth, synapses are overproduced and refined by patterned activity, while myelination and network specialisation continue for decades. Sensitive periods are times when particular experience has unusually strong effects, but they are not always absolute deadlines. Severe deprivation can alter development, yet later enriched experience may permit substantial recovery depending on timing, duration, system, and individual biology.

Infants regulate arousal and distress through interaction with caregivers before they can do so independently. Attachment describes an organised pattern for seeking safety and using a familiar caregiver as a secure base, not a fixed personality label or simple measure of parental love. Caregiver availability, infant temperament, stress, culture, and context shape observed behaviour. Secure relationships support exploration and recovery from distress, while atypical patterns may reflect adaptation to inconsistent or frightening environments rather than deliberate choice.

Temperament refers to early individual differences in reactivity, attention, activity, and self-regulation. It has biological continuity but is shaped by experience. Goodness of fit describes how well environmental expectations and support match the child's style. A highly reactive child may struggle in an unpredictable setting but thrive with preparation and calm routines. Labelling temperament as difficult can obscure the interaction between person and environment and encourage adults to treat a probabilistic tendency as destiny.

Motor development depends on nervous-system maturation, body proportions, muscle strength, sensory feedback, motivation, and opportunity to practise. Infants do not merely execute a prewritten sequence; they discover stable solutions to changing body and environmental constraints. New locomotion changes what can be seen, reached, and socially shared, thereby altering cognitive experience. Assessment should consider vision, hearing, tone, asymmetry, pain, cardiopulmonary endurance, and cultural handling practices rather than viewing motor delay in isolation.

Language develops through biological preparedness and social learning. Infants discriminate speech patterns, share attention, take conversational turns, map words to referents, and infer grammatical regularities. Receptive language generally precedes expressive language. Joint attention and gesture connect another person's focus with objects and words. Quantity of speech exposure matters less than responsive, meaningful interaction alone would suggest; overheard or passive media language does not provide the same contingent feedback. Multilingual exposure does not inherently cause language disorder.

Conceptual development changes how children represent objects, causes, minds, quantity, and rules. Young children can reason impressively within familiar contexts while failing tasks that demand language, inhibition, or unusual instructions. Stage theories capture broad qualitative shifts but often underestimate early competence and variation. Knowledge is domain-specific: expertise in a familiar area can support reasoning beyond what age alone predicts. Development therefore combines gradual accumulation, strategy change, and occasional reorganisation rather than one uniform ascent.

Executive functions include inhibition, working-memory updating, flexible switching, planning, and monitoring. They depend on distributed frontoparietal, subcortical, and cerebellar networks and develop through childhood and adolescence. Performance is strongly affected by sleep, stress, motivation, task familiarity, and environmental structure. A child who succeeds one-to-one in a quiet room may struggle in a noisy classroom without contradiction. Support can externalise executive demands through routines, visual cues, smaller steps, and immediate feedback.

Theory of mind is the capacity to represent mental states such as belief, desire, knowledge, and intention. It develops through language, social interaction, executive control, and cultural practice. Passing a false-belief task is one milestone, not the entirety of social understanding. Real social cognition requires reading ambiguous cues, integrating history, recognising irony, regulating one's own emotion, and revising interpretations. Neurodevelopmental differences may change these processes without implying absence of empathy or moral concern.

Moral development involves emotion, social learning, reasoning, identity, and institutions. Children learn norms through consequences and imitation, but they also distinguish many moral harms from arbitrary conventions. With development, reasoning can expand from avoiding punishment toward reciprocity, social order, rights, and principles, although people use several modes depending on context. Sophisticated moral language does not guarantee behaviour when power, group loyalty, fatigue, threat, or incentives pull in another direction.

Adolescence combines pubertal biological change with expanding cognitive, social, and legal roles. Reward and social-affective systems can become highly responsive before regulatory systems are fully mature, especially in emotionally charged peer contexts. This does not make adolescents uniformly irrational. They often reason like adults in calm settings, learn rapidly, and adapt to local incentives. Exploration and risk taking can support independence but become harmful when environments offer high-intensity rewards, low supervision, chronic stress, or easy access to lethal means.

Identity development integrates values, commitments, social roles, body, culture, and imagined future. Exploration without commitment and commitment without exploration can both be temporary phases. Sexuality, gender, ethnicity, disability, faith, and occupation may become more or less central across contexts. Supportive environments permit exploration without coercion or rejection. Distress can arise from internal conflict, interpersonal harm, discrimination, or unsafe conditions, and should not automatically be attributed to the identity itself.

Adult development includes changing intimacy, work, caregiving, generativity, and adaptation to gains and losses. Cognitive performance does not move in one direction. Processing speed and some aspects of novel problem solving tend to decline gradually from early adulthood, while knowledge, vocabulary, and expertise can remain stable or grow. Strategy, education, health, sensory function, and occupational demands shape trajectories. Cross-sectional age differences can reflect cohort history rather than ageing, while longitudinal studies can be biased by selective survival and repeated testing.

Normal cognitive ageing includes slower retrieval and greater vulnerability to divided attention, but it does not imply inevitable dementia. Older adults may compensate by using knowledge, routines, external aids, and bilateral networks. Hearing or visual loss can masquerade as cognitive impairment and can also increase true cognitive load and social isolation. Acute decline suggests delirium, illness, medication, or another reversible disturbance until assessed. Progressive interference with independent function requires evaluation beyond reassurance about normal ageing.

Socioemotional priorities can change as perceived future time narrows. Older adults may select fewer emotionally meaningful relationships and regulate affect effectively despite physical loss. Grief is an adaptive response whose course varies; it should not be reduced to a mandatory sequence of stages. Bereavement can coexist with relief, anger, guilt, meaning, and continued connection. Persistent severe dysfunction or danger warrants attention, but variation in expression across people and cultures is expected.

Development is embedded in nested systems. Family resources, neighbourhood safety, education, health care, law, discrimination, conflict, and economic policy shape daily inputs to the nervous system. Chronic adversity can alter stress physiology and opportunity, but statistical associations do not make outcomes inevitable. Protective relationships, material support, predictable routines, community belonging, and accessible services can buffer risk. Describing resilience should not shift responsibility from harmful systems onto individuals expected to endure them.

Developmental categories are useful when they explain needs and open support, but harmful when treated as complete identities. Diagnostic thresholds divide continuous traits and are influenced by age, culture, demands, and measurement. Masking or compensation can conceal difficulty at substantial cost. Strengths may coexist with impairment. Good formulation describes the person's profile, context, goals, and required accommodations while remaining open to change rather than merely assigning a label.

Across the lifespan, development is best understood as probabilistic adaptation. Earlier experience constrains but does not wholly determine later function. Biology creates opportunities and vulnerabilities; relationships and institutions distribute practice, safety, and stress. Clinical reasoning compares a person with their own trajectory as well as population expectations, separates difference from disorder, and identifies modifiable barriers that can improve participation at the current stage of life.

## TTS module 3: Stress, motivation, habits, and behaviour change

Stress is the process through which perceived demands mobilise adaptation. A stressor is an event or condition; stress is the organism's response and interpretation. The same event can be experienced as threat, challenge, loss, or irrelevance according to predictability, control, resources, learning, and social meaning. Acute stress can improve survival and performance by prioritising attention and energy. Harm emerges when activation is extreme, repeated, prolonged, poorly matched to the demand, or followed by inadequate recovery.

Rapid stress responses involve sympathetic and adrenal-medullary activation. Noradrenaline changes alertness and vascular tone, while adrenaline supports cardiac output, ventilation, glucose availability, and redistribution of flow. Slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activation releases corticotropin-releasing signals, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol. Cortisol mobilises substrates, alters immunity, affects memory, and feeds back to brain and pituitary. Circadian rhythm and pulsatile secretion mean one cortisol measurement is difficult to interpret without timing and clinical context.

Allostasis is stability achieved through change: heart rate, blood pressure, metabolism, vigilance, and immune activity adjust to anticipated demand. Allostatic load describes cumulative physiological cost when mediators are repeatedly activated, fail to shut off, or compensate inefficiently. It is a conceptual framework rather than one universally standardised clinical test. Poverty, discrimination, unsafe work, caregiving burden, chronic illness, isolation, and sleep disruption can create sustained demand, so stress should not be reduced to an individual's attitude.

Appraisal influences response. Primary appraisal concerns what is at stake; secondary appraisal concerns available options and coping resources. Problem-focused coping changes the stressor, emotion-focused coping changes emotional response, and meaning-focused coping places the event within values or purpose. None is universally superior. Direct action is useful when a problem is controllable, while acceptance or emotional regulation may be adaptive when it is not. Avoidance can provide short relief yet maintain fear or allow practical problems to grow.

Perceived control often reduces stress, but control that is illusory or accompanied by blame can be harmful. Predictability permits preparation, though reliable anticipation of an unavoidable aversive event can itself prolong distress. Social support can provide practical help, information, belonging, validation, and physiological buffering. Support quality matters more than mere contact. Advice that ignores a person's goals, privacy, culture, or autonomy may become another demand rather than a resource.

Motivation describes processes that initiate, direct, and sustain action. Drives arise partly from physiological states, incentives from expected external outcomes, and goals from represented future states. Dopamine contributes to learning which cues and actions predict reward, but it is not a simple pleasure chemical. Wanting, liking, effort, and learning can dissociate. A cue may acquire intense motivational pull even when consumption provides little pleasure, an important feature of addiction and compulsive behaviour.

Expectancy-value accounts propose that action depends on expected success and the value of the outcome, modified by cost. A person may value health yet expect failure, or believe change is possible but judge the effort, money, side effects, stigma, or inconvenience too high. Information about risk changes only one component. Effective formulation asks what outcome matters, what the person predicts will happen, and which immediate costs dominate the distant benefit.

Self-efficacy is confidence in the ability to perform a specific behaviour under specified conditions. It grows through successful practice, credible modelling, useful encouragement, and interpretation of physiological states. It is not generic self-esteem. Goals that are specific and challenging can guide effort when they remain attainable and feedback is available. Very broad goals such as becoming healthy provide direction but not an executable action. Breaking them into observable steps creates opportunities for mastery and revision.

Self-determination theory distinguishes autonomous motivation, in which action feels chosen and aligned with values, from controlled motivation driven by pressure, shame, or contingent approval. Competence, autonomy, and relatedness support sustained engagement. External rewards can help initiate behaviour but may undermine intrinsic interest when experienced as controlling. In medicine, informed choice is not passive abandonment: clinicians can recommend strongly while preserving agency, explaining reasons, and adapting the plan to the patient's priorities.

Habits are cue-linked response tendencies acquired through repetition in a stable context. They reduce deliberative load and can persist after the outcome loses value. A goal may start an action, but repeated performance at the same time and place allows environmental cues to gain control. Changing knowledge alone then has limited effect. Behaviour can be redesigned by altering cues, friction, sequence, and immediate reinforcement, or by attaching a new action to an existing routine.

Implementation intentions specify the link between a cue and an action: when a defined situation occurs, the person will perform a defined behaviour. They convert a distant intention into a retrievable rule and are most useful when obstacles are anticipated. Action planning states where, when, and how; coping planning states what to do when a barrier appears. Plans must remain flexible enough for illness, caregiving, shift work, cost, and fluctuating capacity.

The capability-opportunity-motivation model treats behaviour as emerging when a person has physical and psychological capability, social and material opportunity, and reflective or automatic motivation. This prevents motivational explanations from swallowing structural barriers. A person cannot follow advice that is unaffordable, inaccessible, unsafe, physically impossible, or incompatible with work. Training helps a capability gap; reminders help a memory gap; environmental redesign helps an opportunity gap; neither moral exhortation nor education fixes all three.

Stage models describe movement through lack of current intention, consideration, preparation, action, and maintenance. They remind clinicians to match support to readiness, but people do not always progress in order and boundaries are imprecise. Treating stage assignment as a diagnosis can oversimplify ambivalence. Motivational interviewing instead uses collaborative conversation to explore mixed motives, elicit the person's own reasons for change, and avoid reflexive argument. It respects autonomy while drawing attention to discrepancy between current behaviour and valued goals.

Risk perception depends on more than numerical probability. People respond to immediacy, vividness, dread, familiarity, perceived control, and trust. Relative risk without baseline risk can exaggerate benefit or harm, while tiny probabilities may be ignored or overweighted. Presenting absolute frequencies with the same denominator, relevant time period, and balanced outcomes improves understanding. Emotional meaning still matters, and comprehension should be checked by asking the person to explain the choice in their own words.

Behavioural economics highlights predictable effects of defaults, present bias, loss aversion, social norms, and limited attention. Defaults can increase uptake by making one option easiest, but ethical use requires transparency, easy refusal, and alignment with welfare rather than institutional convenience. Incentives may be useful, especially for immediate reinforcement of delayed health benefits, but can be coercive when resources are scarce. A nudge should not conceal alternatives or substitute for removing genuine barriers.

Relapse is common because old cue-response pathways, rewards, stressors, and social contexts persist. It is information about the plan and environment, not proof of moral failure. Lapse management aims to prevent one event from becoming complete abandonment through rapid review, self-compassion, and a concrete restart. Maintenance improves when the behaviour becomes rewarding, identity-consistent, socially supported, and resilient to routine disruption. Periodic review is necessary because goals and circumstances change.

Stress and behaviour influence each other bidirectionally. Stress can narrow attention toward immediate relief, reduce working memory, disrupt sleep, and strengthen habitual responding. Behaviours such as activity, regular sleep opportunity, social contact, substance use, avoidance, and help-seeking alter later stress. Recommendations must avoid promising that lifestyle alone can remove structural adversity or cure disease. Small behavioural changes can still improve function and agency when embedded within appropriate medical and social support.

Behaviour-change interventions should specify mechanism and outcome. Did they improve knowledge, confidence, access, action frequency, a biomarker, symptoms, or long-term health? Engagement is not itself benefit, and short-term adherence may not persist. Evaluation should monitor unequal burden and unintended effects, including stigma, surveillance, opportunity cost, and widening disparities. Co-design with affected people can expose practical constraints that theory misses.

The practical synthesis is to analyse behaviour rather than label character. Define the action and context, identify capability and opportunity, understand expected rewards and costs, map cues and consequences, and assess stress and recovery. Then choose the smallest mechanism-matched intervention, measure whether it worked, and revise. Sustainable change is more likely when it is feasible, meaningful, repeated in a supportive environment, and recoverable after interruption.

# Chapter 100: Social Psychology, Communication, Culture, and the Behaviour of Health

## TTS module 1: Social cognition, identity, influence, and groups

Social psychology studies how thought, feeling, and behaviour are shaped by actual, imagined, or implied others. Medical decisions are never purely individual calculations. Patients interpret symptoms through family and cultural expectations, clinicians work within teams and hierarchies, and institutions define which actions are easy, rewarded, visible, or prohibited. Social processes can coordinate care and provide belonging, but they can also create bias, silence disagreement, and distribute harm. Understanding them does not imply that behaviour is irrational; social information is often essential evidence about danger, trust, and acceptable action.

Social perception begins with rapid categorisation. Faces, voices, clothing, roles, and context activate expectations that guide attention and interpretation. Categories reduce cognitive load but can obscure within-group variation. A stereotype is a belief about a group, prejudice is an evaluative attitude, and discrimination is behaviour or institutional practice that creates unequal treatment. These components can occur separately. A person may explicitly reject prejudice while learned associations or organisational routines still produce unequal decisions.

Attribution concerns how people explain behaviour. Observers often overemphasise stable personal traits and underweight situational constraints, especially when those constraints are invisible. Actors have more access to their circumstances and may explain the same behaviour through workload, fear, or limited options. In health care, missed appointments can be labelled irresponsibility when transport, shift work, disability, childcare, cost, or prior mistreatment is causal. A useful formulation tests both person-level and environment-level explanations.

Attribution is also influenced by outcome knowledge. Once a diagnosis or adverse event is known, earlier ambiguous signs can appear obvious, a hindsight bias that exaggerates predictability. The just-world tendency can lead observers to assume that people deserve outcomes, protecting a sense of order at the cost of blaming illness or trauma on behaviour. Self-serving attributions credit success to ability and assign failure to circumstance, though depression, shame, and marginalisation can reverse this pattern.

Attitudes include cognitive beliefs, emotional evaluations, and action tendencies, but they predict behaviour best when they are specific, accessible, stable, and relevant to the situation. General approval of exercise does not guarantee walking today in unsafe weather. Behaviour can also change attitudes. When people act in a way inconsistent with their self-concept, cognitive dissonance creates discomfort that may be reduced by changing behaviour, changing beliefs, adding justification, or avoiding information. Coercive public commitment can therefore entrench resistance rather than create genuine agreement.

Persuasion depends on source, message, audience, channel, and context. Careful processing evaluates evidence when motivation and capacity are high; heuristic processing uses cues such as expertise, familiarity, emotion, or social endorsement when attention is limited. Both can be adaptive. Credibility requires perceived competence and trustworthiness, and conflicts of interest can undermine either. Fear messages work poorly when threat is emphasised without an effective, feasible response; defensive avoidance becomes more likely when efficacy is low.

Social norms describe perceived behaviour or approval. Descriptive norms concern what others do, while injunctive norms concern what others approve. Correcting an exaggerated belief that harmful behaviour is universal can reduce it. However, advertising the high prevalence of misconduct may unintentionally normalise it unless paired with a clear valued standard. Norms are reference-group specific: the behaviour of trusted peers often matters more than that of society in general.

Conformity can arise from informational influence, when others are treated as evidence, or normative influence, when agreement protects belonging and avoids rejection. Uncertainty, unanimity, public responding, and group importance strengthen conformity. One visible dissenter can reduce pressure even if their answer differs from ours because unanimity has been broken. In clinical teams, deliberately inviting independent assessments before discussion can reduce early anchoring on the senior person's view.

Compliance is responding to a request, whereas obedience involves a perceived authority command. Small initial commitments can increase later consistency; very large requests can make a subsequent smaller request seem reasonable; scarcity and reciprocity can also influence decisions. These techniques are not inherently deceptive, but asymmetries of knowledge and power make their use in medicine ethically sensitive. Consent requires more than obtaining a yes through social pressure.

Authority can coordinate expertise and accountability, yet it also makes harmful action easier when responsibility feels transferred upward, tasks are fragmented, and dissent seems disloyal. Professional status does not eliminate this vulnerability. Clear escalation pathways, graded assertiveness, closed-loop communication, and leaders who thank people for raising concerns make safety objections more actionable. A culture that formally permits speaking up but punishes it socially has not solved the problem.

Group identity provides meaning, mutual aid, and expectations. People categorise themselves and others into in-groups and out-groups, often favouring their own group even when distinctions are arbitrary. Threat, competition, and unequal status can intensify boundaries. Cross-group contact can reduce prejudice when participants have meaningful cooperation, supported equality, and institutional backing; mere proximity under hostile conditions may reinforce stereotypes. Individuals hold multiple intersecting identities, so one category rarely predicts experience completely.

Deindividuation occurs when anonymity, arousal, group immersion, or reduced accountability shifts behaviour toward salient local norms. It does not inevitably produce aggression; a prosocial group norm can also become stronger. Diffusion of responsibility can reduce helping when many bystanders assume someone else will act. Explicitly assigning a person a task counters ambiguity. In emergencies, saying a named person should call for help is more effective than addressing an undefined crowd.

Group polarisation occurs when discussion shifts members toward a more extreme version of their initial tendency. Members hear more arguments supporting the shared direction and compare themselves with the group norm. Groupthink describes defective decision processes in cohesive groups under pressure, including suppressed doubt, incomplete alternatives, and illusions of consensus. Cohesion itself is not the cause; directive leadership, insulation, homogeneity, and lack of method create risk. Structured dissent and independent review improve decisions without requiring interpersonal hostility.

Collective intelligence depends less on the single smartest member than on information sharing, turn-taking, psychological safety, and task-relevant expertise. Groups often discuss information everyone already knows while unique information remains unspoken. A shared-information bias can make meetings feel consensual while missing the decisive fact. Asking each member what evidence would change the plan, and recording unresolved disagreement, makes hidden information easier to surface.

Social loafing is reduced effort when individual contribution is unidentifiable, whereas coordination loss occurs when capable individuals interfere with one another. Clear roles and visible interdependence can reduce both. Competition can increase effort on simple tasks but suppress learning, candour, and help-seeking. Health-care teams need shared goals and role clarity while preserving enough redundancy to catch error. Removing all overlap may improve apparent efficiency but destroy resilience.

Power is the capacity to shape outcomes, resources, attention, or norms. It can arise from expertise, formal position, rewards, coercion, relationships, or control of information. Power changes interaction: high-power individuals may speak more, receive more agreement, and notice constraints less, while low-power individuals monitor others closely and bear greater risk from conflict. A patient's apparent agreement may therefore reflect dependence rather than preference. Clinicians should create private opportunities for questions and make refusal genuinely safe.

Prosocial behaviour is influenced by empathy, identity, norms, cost, reciprocity, and perceived efficacy. Empathic concern can motivate help, but distress focused on one's own discomfort can prompt withdrawal. Repeated exposure to suffering does not mechanically extinguish compassion; exhaustion, moral distress, insufficient resources, and defensive coping are distinct mechanisms. Organisational support, manageable demands, peer connection, and meaningful efficacy matter more than exhorting clinicians to be resilient.

Conflict can concern tasks, processes, values, identity, or relationships. Task disagreement can improve reasoning when psychological safety and shared purpose are strong, but personal contempt impairs cooperation. Negotiation distinguishes positions from underlying interests and seeks options that meet several interests where possible. Some conflicts reflect genuine scarcity or incompatible values and cannot be transformed into simple win-win solutions. Fair procedure, transparency, and review remain important when everyone cannot receive their preferred outcome.

Social cognition is contextual and probabilistic. Biases are not defects possessed only by other people, and education about them rarely abolishes them. Better environments slow high-risk decisions, expose relevant base rates, invite independent views, document reasons, and audit outcomes across groups. The goal is not to remove social influence from medicine, which is impossible, but to make beneficial influence visible and accountable while limiting conformity, hierarchy, categorisation, and power from silently determining care.

## TTS module 2: Culture, language, stigma, and clinical communication

Culture is a dynamic set of learned meanings, practices, relationships, and institutions through which people interpret experience. It is not a fixed list of traits attached to ethnicity. People participate in several cultures shaped by family, language, religion, profession, generation, migration, disability, sexuality, class, and place, and their identification changes by context. Cultural humility means sustained curiosity, self-reflection, attention to power, and willingness to repair misunderstanding rather than claiming mastery of another person's group.

Illness is the person's lived experience of symptoms and disruption, while disease refers to a professional account of altered biology. The two overlap but are not identical. Patients and clinicians may hold different explanatory models about cause, timing, severity, bodily mechanism, appropriate treatment, and expected outcome. Asking what the person calls the problem, what they fear, why they think it began, and what help they expect reveals clinically relevant information without assuming that one model is irrational.

Traditional, complementary, religious, and biomedical practices may coexist. A person may use prayer, dietary rules, herbal products, family advice, and prescribed medicine for different purposes. Dismissal can drive practices underground and hide interactions, while uncritical acceptance can overlook toxicity or delayed effective care. Respectful inquiry asks what is used, how it is prepared, who recommended it, what benefit is sought, and whether the person is willing to coordinate it with treatment. Respect applies to the person; factual claims remain open to evidence.

Structural competence extends attention from interpersonal culture to institutions that produce health. Housing, immigration rules, policing, education, labour conditions, transport, food systems, environmental exposure, and access to care shape what choices are available. A clinician cannot individually repair every structure, but can avoid mislabelling constrained behaviour as preference, document relevant barriers, connect resources, adapt plans, and support system-level improvement. Cultural explanations should not conceal material deprivation or discrimination.

Language discordance changes diagnostic accuracy, consent, safety, and trust. A trained interpreter conveys content and pragmatic meaning, manages turn-taking, and clarifies ambiguity while preserving the speakers' ownership of the conversation. Family members may offer valuable support but can filter information, introduce conflict, or be inappropriate for sensitive matters. Children should not bear responsibility for interpreting consequential medical information. Automated translation may assist limited tasks but requires caution where nuance, privacy, or risk is high.

When using an interpreter, clinicians should address and look toward the patient, use first-person speech, pause in manageable segments, and avoid side conversations. The interpreter should receive enough context to anticipate specialised language, and uncertainty should be made explicit. A longer translated exchange is not evidence of inaccuracy; some concepts require explanation rather than word substitution. Documentation should record interpreter involvement and modality, not treat the interpreter as the person who consented.

Health literacy is the capacity to find, understand, evaluate, and use health information within a particular task and system. It is relational: even highly educated people may struggle when frightened, ill, in pain, using an unfamiliar language, or facing opaque forms. Universal precautions assume that anyone may benefit from plain communication. This avoids singling out and shaming people through informal literacy tests. Plain language keeps the necessary precision while reducing avoidable complexity.

Communication should prioritise a small number of actionable ideas, explain unfamiliar terms, connect numbers to decisions, and use diagrams or demonstrations when appropriate. Teach-back asks the person to explain the plan in their own words so the clinician can test the explanation, not the patient's intelligence. A neutral prompt makes repair safer. Return demonstration is particularly useful for devices, injections, wound care, and emergency actions. Written material should reinforce rather than replace dialogue.

Nonverbal communication includes gaze, facial expression, posture, distance, touch, silence, pacing, and tone. Meanings vary by person and culture, so one sign should not be overinterpreted. Lack of eye contact may reflect respect, anxiety, pain, neurodevelopmental style, trauma, or visual impairment rather than deception. Clinicians can observe a mismatch between words and affect while asking open clarification. Physical positioning at the same level and reducing interruptions can communicate attention without adding consultation time substantially.

Stigma marks an attribute as socially discrediting and operates through labelling, stereotyping, separation, status loss, and discrimination under unequal power. It can be public, anticipated, experienced, or internalised, and can attach to mental illness, infection, weight, substance use, disability, poverty, sexuality, or many other conditions. Anticipated judgement delays care and reduces disclosure. Clinical language that turns a person into a diagnosis or moral category can reproduce stigma even when no insult is intended.

Person-first and identity-first language preferences differ. Some people prefer a person with a condition; others claim an identity as a valued community membership. The safest approach is to ask or follow the person's language where feasible, while avoiding terms that imply blame or contamination. More important than vocabulary alone is whether care respects autonomy, provides access, and avoids lower-quality treatment. Polite language cannot compensate for discriminatory decisions.

Implicit bias refers to associations that can influence perception or behaviour without deliberate endorsement. Bias may affect pain assessment, credibility, diagnostic thresholds, communication, and referral. Individual awareness training has limited effect when workflows still permit unchecked discretion or encode historical inequity. Standardised evidence-based criteria, decision support with audited performance, diverse teams, adequate time, and outcome monitoring can reduce opportunities for bias. Algorithms require the same scrutiny because biased data and proxy variables can automate disparity.

Trauma-informed care recognises that past or current trauma may shape safety, trust, bodily responses, and control. It does not require every patient to disclose trauma. Predictability, explanation before touch, meaningful choice, privacy, collaboration, and permission to pause reduce avoidable threat. A behaviour that appears difficult may be a protective response to loss of control. Trauma-informed practice is compatible with firm boundaries and urgent action, but explains necessity and restores choice as soon as possible.

Open questions invite a narrative, while focused closed questions clarify details. Reflective listening checks meaning and emotion rather than merely repeating words. Summaries organise the account and offer a chance for correction. Premature interruption can redirect the history before the patient's priorities emerge, yet an entirely unstructured interview can miss safety-critical information. Skilled communication moves deliberately between open exploration and focused testing and makes the transition explicit.

Empathy is communicating an accurate effort to understand another person's perspective and emotion. It does not require experiencing the same feeling or agreeing with every interpretation. Naming a likely emotion should remain tentative, allowing correction. Validation acknowledges that a response is understandable in context without confirming an inaccurate factual belief. Reassurance before understanding can feel dismissive; realistic reassurance identifies what is known, what will be done, and how uncertainty will be managed.

Bad news is information that substantially alters a person's expected future. Preparation includes privacy, sufficient time, relevant support people, and knowledge of current facts. The clinician should assess what the person understands and how much detail they want, give a warning that difficult information is coming, use direct language, pause, respond to emotion, and then discuss next steps. Euphemism can create confusion, but excessive detail immediately after shock may not be retained. Follow-up allows information to be revisited.

Conflict often reflects unmet needs, fear, inconsistent information, prior harm, or incompatible goals rather than a simple communication defect. De-escalation lowers immediate threat through calm pacing, space, respect, clear limits, and choices where possible. Safety takes priority when violence is imminent. After stabilisation, identifying the underlying concern is more useful than debating every accusation. Apology can acknowledge harm and responsibility; defensive technical explanation before recognition often intensifies conflict.

Confidentiality supports disclosure, but its limits should be explained rather than silently assumed. Privacy may be compromised when family members answer, portals share access, or consultations occur in crowded settings. Sensitive questions are best normalised and asked privately when possible. Shared cultural background does not guarantee trust, and small communities can heighten fear of recognition. Communication systems must protect information as well as clinicians promise to do so.

Effective communication is not an ornamental interpersonal skill added after diagnosis. It changes the data obtained, the interpretation of symptoms, the validity of consent, the feasibility of treatment, and whether harm is detected. Cultural humility, language access, structural awareness, stigma reduction, and clear dialogue all improve epistemic quality: they make the clinical account more accurate. The final test is whether patient and clinician share enough understanding to act safely while preserving dignity and the person's legitimate authority over their life.

## TTS module 3: Adherence, placebo and nocebo, risk, consent, and shared decisions

Adherence describes how a person's medication use or health behaviour corresponds with an agreed plan. It is preferable to compliance when it preserves collaboration, but terminology does not guarantee respect. A plan can fail because it is ineffective, unaffordable, confusing, burdensome, culturally unacceptable, physically difficult, or inconsistent with the person's goals. Calling someone nonadherent without identifying the behaviour and reason turns an outcome into a character judgment and blocks useful intervention.

Treatment-taking has several phases. Initiation is whether treatment begins, implementation is how actual use corresponds to the regimen, and persistence is how long treatment continues. A person may fill a prescription but never start, take it inconsistently, use it correctly and later stop, or deliberately adjust it according to symptoms. Each pattern has different causes and solutions.
